title: RBI Deploys Bond Sales and Rupee Defenses as Currency Tests Record Lows
excerpt: A ₹250 billion bond sale, a CRR squeeze and a weekend FX package sent the rupee up 1% Monday — the RBI is now tightening on three fronts at once.
body:
• The Reserve Bank of India stacked two interventions in three days: a ₹250 billion ($2.58 billion) bond sale announced Friday, and a weekend foreign-exchange package that sent the rupee surging ~1% to 95.76 per dollar at Monday's open.
  • Friday's moves also raised the daily cash-reserve-ratio maintenance requirement from 90% to 99% of the requirement — locking up an estimated ₹1 lakh crore in additional daily reserves — after a record ₹1 trillion in net bond sales in September.
  • The weekend FX package gives oil companies a special dollar window, bars firms from rebooking cancelled rupee-linked derivatives, and imposes a 20% cash requirement on certain FX contracts above $2 million — raising the cost of betting against the rupee.
  • What this means for you: the rupee's slide (down ~7% this year, near its 96.96 record low) is the RBI's top worry; NRIs timing remittances should note the central bank is actively leaning against further weakness — Monday's 1% rally is the intervention working.

The Reserve Bank of India spent the weekend fighting a two-front war — against a sagging rupee and a flooded banking system — and by Monday morning the rupee was winning its battle. The currency surged about 1% to 95.76 per dollar at the open after the RBI unveiled a package of foreign-exchange measures, Reuters reported, reversing a 0.4% slide last week that had taken it to 96.73, within touching distance of the all-time low of 96.96 hit in May.

Friday: draining the flood

The first move came Friday, when the RBI announced an open-market bond sale of ₹250 billion ($2.58 billion) for Tuesday, spanning maturities from FY2030 to FY2035. It follows a record ₹1 trillion in net bond sales in September — the highest in over a decade — as the central bank mops up a liquidity surplus that has averaged more than ₹7 trillion a day since September 1, about 2.6% of deposits.

"Friday: draining the flood The first move came Friday, when the RBI announced an open-market bond sale of ₹250 billion ($2.58 billion) for Tuesday, spanning maturities from FY2030 to FY2035."

The same day, the RBI raised the daily cash-reserve-ratio maintenance requirement from 90% to 99% of the requirement, effective October 16. Banks park 3% of deposits under CRR at zero interest; the shift locks up an estimated ₹1 lakh crore in additional daily reserves. Governor Sanjay Malhotra had signaled the move, saying the liquidity surge "would not be a long-term phenomenon." ICICI Securities PD estimates the surplus could fall below 1% of deposits, into the 0–0.5% range.

The weekend: defending the rupee

Saturday brought the currency package. Its centerpiece: a special window for oil companies — India's largest dollar buyers — to purchase dollars directly, diverting their demand away from the spot market. The RBI also barred firms from rebooking cancelled rupee-linked derivatives, slashed the threshold for transactions without underlying exposure, and imposed a 20% cash requirement — effectively a CRR — on certain FX contracts above $2 million. The mechanism is straightforward: make it more expensive to bet against the rupee, and the speculative pressure eases. Citi noted the package raises the near-term cost of rupee-depreciation trades.

The measures land against a grim backdrop. The rupee is down 6.6–7% this year, foreign investors have sold roughly $29 billion of Indian equities, and a Reuters poll of 35 strategists in early October put the currency at 96.10 in three months and 96.50 by end-March — with 97.50 in a year, and 100 per dollar within six months at the current pace of about 1% a month.

Bonds feel the squeeze

The bond market is caught in the crossfire. The benchmark 6.94% 2036 yield ended Friday at 7.2994% and is expected to trade 7.26–7.32% this week — mild selling pressure from the OMO supply, though a firmer rupee could ease foreign investors' fears of currency losses on their bond holdings. ICICI Securities PD notes the OMO sales have led to a bear flattening of the yield curve. Reuters' Friday coverage details the liquidity arithmetic.

Why this matters

Context is everything: days earlier, the RBI raised its key policy rate for the first time in nearly four years, signaling more hikes to come. The central bank is now tightening on three fronts at once — rates, liquidity and the currency — an unusually aggressive posture that shows how seriously it takes the rupee's slide. For the diaspora, the stakes are concrete: every point the rupee loses against the dollar erodes the value of India-bound remittances and NRI deposits, while higher domestic yields slowly improve returns on NRE fixed deposits. The RBI's message this weekend was unambiguous — it will not let the currency drift. Whether markets believe it past Monday's rally is the next question.
